story.title: Renewed Fighting Erupts in Northern Ethiopia as Tigray Rebels Declare War
story.summary: Fighting has intensified in northern Ethiopia as Tigray's rebel authorities declare a 'full-blown war' against the Ethiopian government. The Ethiopian army reports that 272 Tigrayan fighters have been killed and 260 wounded during a counter-offensive in the Amhara region, although these figures have not been independently verified. The conflict is also spreading into neighboring regions, raising concerns of a potential humanitarian crisis similar to the previous civil war.

timeline_highlights.summary: Tigrayan rebels have taken control of airports in northern Ethiopia and engaged in clashes with federal troops in the Afar region. timeline_highlights.title: Ethiopia's Tigray Rebels Declare Full-Blown War Amid Intensifying Conflict
timeline_highlights.summary: Tigray rebels in Ethiopia have declared a state of 'full-blown war' against the federal government, marking a significant escalation in ongoing tensions. Reports indicate that heavy artillery attacks are occurring in neighboring states, with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) claiming to have seized control of the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region. The Ethiopian army has stated that it killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 during a counter-offensive in Amhara, although these figures have not been independently verified.

event_overview.title: About Ethiopia Conflict
event_overview.subject: Ethiopia Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Ethiopia conflict refers here to the armed and political crisis centered on the Tigray region in northern Ethiopia, principally involving Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), with major effects across neighboring Afar and Amhara. The large-scale war that began in November 2020 was followed by an African Union-mediated permanent cessation-of-hostilities agreement in November 2022, but unresolved security, territorial, humanitarian and accountability issues have left the situation vulnerable to renewed violence.

facts.label: Conflict period
facts.value: Large-scale fighting in the Tigray war began in November 2020; the UN’s international commission documented major phases of fighting through the November 2, 2022 cessation-of-hostilities agreement.

facts.label: Core parties and armed actors
facts.value: The Pretoria agreement was signed by the Government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia and the TPLF. The wider war also involved Ethiopian federal and regional forces, Eritrean forces and local militias at different times.

facts.label: Peace agreement
facts.value: African Union-led talks in Pretoria, South Africa, produced the Agreement for Lasting Peace through a Permanent Cessation of Hostilities on November 2, 2022. Its stated objectives included stopping hostilities, enabling humanitarian access, restoring services, and supporting reconciliation and implementation measures.

facts.label: Outstanding issues
facts.value: Implementation of the agreement has been tied to disarmament, humanitarian access, restoration of services, return of displaced people, transitional justice and the status of forces in parts of Tigray; UN reporting found that the agreement had not yet produced a sustainable settlement.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the reported renewal of fighting in northern Ethiopia from September 23-25, 2026; it does not attempt to catalog the full 2020-22 war, all armed groups, or separate conflicts elsewhere in Ethiopia.

explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground?
explore_lenses.title: Fighting spread beyond Tigray and disrupted air links
explore_lenses.summary: The escalation is no longer confined to localized clashes inside Tigray: fighting has been reported in Tigray, Amhara and Afar, while Tigrayan forces seized three civilian airports. The reported battlefield casualty figures remain unverified.

claims.text: The UN and African Union said Tigrayan forces seized or occupied the civilian airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian air services.

Human Rights Watch reported that fighting involving Ethiopia’s military and forces aligned with the TPLF erupted on September 22 in Tigray, Amhara and Afar, after reported clashes and airstrikes in Tigray since August.
The Ethiopian army’s claim that it killed 272 and wounded 260 Tigrayan fighters in Amhara was reported by AFP, but AFP said it could not independently verify those figures.

points: The UN and African Union said Tigrayan forces seized or occupied the civilian airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian air services.

The Ethiopian army’s claim that it killed 272 and wounded 260 Tigrayan fighters in Amhara was reported by AFP, but AFP said it could not independently verify those figures.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: Access constraints and conflicting accounts from the federal government and Tigrayan authorities make the immediate military picture, territorial control and casualty totals difficult to independently confirm.

explore_lenses.label: How did the conflict reach this point?
explore_lenses.title: A fragile peace process collided with new alliances
explore_lenses.summary: The renewed war follows months of mounting tension despite the November 2022 Pretoria cessation-of-hostilities agreement. The sides give opposing accounts of who began this week’s fighting, while a newly announced armed coalition has broadened the political stakes.

claims.text: The Pretoria agreement, signed by Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF on November 2, 2022, established a permanent cessation-of-hostilities framework and committed the parties to resolve political differences peacefully.

Reuters reported that the outbreak followed months of growing animosity and the TPLF’s announcement days earlier of an alliance with six other armed groups that seeks to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.

Tigray’s leaders say federal forces began a large-scale offensive and that their response is defensive; federal adviser Getachew Reda has accused the TPLF leadership of launching a large-scale attack in Afar and Amhara.

explore_lenses.label: What steps are confirmed next?
explore_lenses.title: AU-led de-escalation efforts are the only announced track
explore_lenses.summary: No ceasefire or talks have been publicly confirmed as of September 25. The concrete diplomatic response so far is an AU push for direct talks under Pretoria, backed by the UN and IGAD, alongside calls to protect civilians and allow aid access.

claims.text: The African Union called for an immediate halt to escalatory actions and a return to direct talks under the Pretoria framework; it said its chairperson asked former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo to urgently engage the parties.
The UN Secretary-General backed the AU effort and called on all parties to de-escalate, protect civilians and ensure safe, unhindered humanitarian access.
IGAD called for a cessation of hostilities and direct dialogue, warning that a return to widespread conflict would have grave consequences for Ethiopia and the wider region.

story_report.summary: Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia has widened beyond Tigray after rebel authorities declared a full-scale war against the federal government. Clashes have spread into the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions, while the Ethiopian army says it killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 in Amhara, figures that have not been independently verified. The escalation has also disrupted civilian aviation and prompted regional and international calls for an immediate de-escalation.

sections.heading: Airport seizures disrupt civilian air services
sections.body: The United Nations and African Union said Tigrayan forces seized or occupied civilian airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting air services. Human Rights Watch said fighting involving Ethiopia’s military and forces aligned with the TPLF erupted on September 22 across Tigray, Amhara and Afar, after reported clashes and airstrikes in Tigray since August. The disruption raises immediate concerns over civilian mobility and humanitarian access.

sections.heading: Pretoria ceasefire framework faces renewed test
sections.body: Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement on November 2, 2022, establishing a permanent cessation-of-hostilities framework and committing both sides to settle political differences peacefully. Reuters reported that the latest outbreak followed months of rising animosity and a TPLF announcement days earlier that it had formed an alliance with six other armed groups seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.

sections.heading: African institutions urge direct negotiations
sections.body: The African Union has called for an immediate halt to escalatory actions and a return to direct talks under the Pretoria framework, with its chairperson asking former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo to urgently engage the parties. The UN secretary-general backed that effort, urging de-escalation, civilian protection and safe humanitarian access. IGAD also called for a cessation of hostilities and dialogue, warning that wider conflict would carry grave consequences for Ethiopia and the region.

unresolved.text: Conflicting accounts and access constraints mean the immediate military situation, territorial control and casualty totals cannot be independently confirmed. There is also no independently established public account of which side initiated the current fighting.
The parties have not publicly committed to talks, and the consulted statements identified no agreed date, venue or participation for negotiations.

related_stories.title: Trump and Xi Conclude Washington Visit with Limited Outcomes
related_stories.summary: President Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state dinner during Xi's first visit to Washington in over a decade. The discussions focused on key issues including trade, Taiwan, Iran, and advancements in artificial intelligence. Despite the high-profile meetings, few concrete achievements were announced following their talks.

related_stories.title: Netanyahu Criticizes UN Delegates Who Walked Out During His Speech
related_stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended Israel's military actions in his speech at the UN General Assembly, labeling delegates who walked out as 'moral cowards.' He dismissed allegations of genocide and reiterated support for operations in Gaza and other regions. The walkout occurred as he addressed the assembly, highlighting tensions surrounding Israel's actions in the Middle East.
